opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the first thing I'd say is that I don't find it very useful to treat "agent" as a binary, where something either is an agent or it isn't. There's been a lot of energy spent on definitional debates, and I think it's more productive to think of agenticness as a spectrum, with a few different dimensions along which a system can be more or less agentic.

One dimension is the environment. How complex and open-ended is the world the system operates in? A system that classifies images is in a narrow, well-defined setting. A system that navigates the web, books things, writes and runs code, or interacts with other people is in a much messier environment, where it can't anticipate everything in advance.

A second dimension is the goals. Is the system given a very specific instruction, like "summarize this document"? Or is it given something underspecified, like "help me plan this trip" or "fix this bug," where it has to figure out what the sub-goals are and how to break the task down?

A third is the degree of independence, or how much human supervision there is. Does a person check every step, or does the system take a long sequence of actions on its own before anyone looks at what it did? Related to that is whether it can take actions with real consequences in the world, like spending money, sending emails, or modifying files, as opposed to just producing text that a human then decides what to do with.

And then there's the architecture: does it use tools, does it plan, does it reflect on its own outputs and retry, does it have memory across steps? Those design patterns tend to correlate with the other dimensions, but I'd treat them as a means rather than the definition.

The reason I like framing it this way is that it ties directly to the practical questions people care about, like how to evaluate these systems and what can go wrong. As you move up along any of these dimensions, evaluation gets harder, because there's more variance in what the system might do. The cost of errors also goes up, because there's less of a human in the loop to catch mistakes. So when someone says "we built an agent," the question I want to ask is: more agentic along which axis, and have you scaled your evaluation and your safeguards accordingly? Often the honest answer is that capability claims have outrun the evidence about reliability. In my view, reliability, not raw capability, is the real bottleneck for agents being useful in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that "agentic" isn't a binary property, it's a spectrum, and it's really a bundle of several distinct dimensions that we tend to lump together.

The first dimension is environment complexity. A system that's operating in a sandboxed, well-specified environment, like solving a math problem or answering a question, is at one end. A system that's operating in an open-ended environment, like the web, or a company's internal software stack, where it has to deal with unanticipated situations, is much further along that axis.

The second is autonomy, and I'd break that down further. There's the question of how long the system operates without human intervention. There's the question of whether it's taking actions in the world, as opposed to just producing text that a human then acts on. Sending an email, making a purchase, executing code, those are consequential actions, and the more a system is doing that without someone checking each step, the more agentic it is in a meaningful sense.

The third dimension is something like the system's internal structure. Does it do planning? Does it use tools? Does it have some kind of memory or state that persists across steps? Does it reflect on its own outputs and try again? These design patterns tend to be present in the systems people call agents, but they're really a means to an end, which is handling the complexity and autonomy I mentioned.

And then there's a fourth thing that I think is underappreciated, which is the interface. Is the human supervising, collaborating, or just delegating? The same underlying system can be more or less agentic depending on how it's deployed. A coding model used in autocomplete mode is not very agentic. The same model told to go fix a bug and open a pull request while you go to lunch is quite agentic.

The reason I think this decomposition matters is that a lot of the hype and a lot of the confusion comes from treating "agent" as a thing you either have or don't. Vendors have an incentive to call everything an agent. But if you ask which of these dimensions a system actually moves along, you get a much clearer picture of both what it can do and where the risks are. The risks scale with autonomy and action-taking in complex environments, not with whether something is branded as an agent.

The other thing I'd say is that the hard part of making systems more agentic is not really the model capabilities, it's reliability. A system that's right ninety percent of the time is great as a question-answering tool, because the human catches the errors. The same error rate compounded over a twenty-step task gives you something that almost never succeeds. So progress on agents is going to look less like dramatic jumps in intelligence and more like the slow engineering work of making each step dependable enough that you can chain them together.

astra-6.text:
I think of agency as a spectrum rather than a binary property. The useful question is: how much autonomy does the system have in pursuing a goal, and what can it actually do in the world?

If I ask a chatbot to draft an email, and then I review it and send it myself, that’s a fairly limited degree of agency. If I give it access to my inbox and say, “Handle scheduling this meeting,” now it has to make a plan, communicate with people, interpret their responses, and decide when the task is done. That’s more agentic because I’ve delegated a goal rather than specified each individual step.

There are several dimensions here: how long it operates without human input, how much discretion it has, what tools it can use, and what consequences its actions can have. Those don’t necessarily move together. A system might have a lot of autonomy within a very narrow, low-stakes task.

So I find it more useful to talk about those concrete dimensions than to ask whether something qualifies as an agent. And agency is distinct from intelligence: giving a system more permissions doesn’t make it more capable of using them well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of agency as a spectrum, rather than a binary property. And the useful question is: how much autonomy does the system have in pursuing a goal? Does it just respond to a prompt, or can it decide what steps to take, use tools, observe the results, and adjust what it does next?

Imagine a system helping you plan a trip. It might suggest an itinerary. Or it might search for flights and hotels. Or you might give it a budget and let it make bookings. Those involve different degrees of agency, even if the underlying language model is the same.

So I would look at the whole system, including the permissions we give it and where we require human approval. A model’s capabilities matter, but so does how we choose to deploy it. And being more agentic doesn’t necessarily mean being more intelligent or more reliable. It means having more latitude to act, which makes the consequences of mistakes especially important.
